query: Consider the following context: During the hot dip aluminum plating process, components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates will come into long-term contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum and be corroded by the aluminum liquid, greatly reducing their service life. In that context, which material can be used for prepare parts for the dipping and plating equipment and protect the equipment from erosion, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) can serve as a protective material for hot dip aluminum plating components because its high melting point and resistance to high‐temperature oxidation allow it to form stable, protective oxide films that act as barriers against erosion by liquid aluminum.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous tungsten-based RHEA with a BCC structure produced by methods such as laser powder bed fusion, ensuring high density and minimal defects.
generation.intervention: Replace conventional steel parts in dipping and plating equipment with parts fabricated from the tungsten-based RHEA.
generation.conditions: Long-term exposure at temperatures near or slightly above the melting point of aluminum (approximately 660–700 °C) under conditions typical of a hot dip aluminum plating process.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a thin, coherent oxide layer (likely tungsten oxide or a mixed oxide) on the surface of the alloy that adheres strongly and resists further penetration of molten aluminum.
generation.mechanism: The refractory nature of tungsten coupled with the high-entropy design promotes both a high melting point and excellent oxidation resistance. When exposed to high-temperature liquid aluminum, a stable oxide scale forms on the RHEA surface, slowing down or preventing chemical interactions and diffusion of aluminum into the protective component.
generation.predicted_outcome: Components made from the tungsten-based RHEA will exhibit significantly reduced erosion (as measured by lower weight loss and surface degradation) compared to conventional materials, thereby extending their service life in the hot dip aluminum plating process.
generation.baseline: Conventional dipping equipment parts (typically made of steel or similar alloys) that show rapid degradation due to direct corrosion by high-temperature liquid aluminum.
generation.boundary: The protective effect is expected to be maintained at temperatures around 660–700 °C in a continuous hot dip environment. Performance could be compromised if oxide scale formation is not uniform or if severe thermal cycling or mechanical stresses cause spallation of the protective layer.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of erosion resistance improvement is uncertain and may depend strongly on the precise alloy composition, processing history, and operating conditions such as thermal cycling and aluminum chemistry.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of roller components: one set using conventional steel and another set using the proposed tungsten-based RHEA. Expose both sets to molten aluminum at 660–700 °C over extended cycles representative of industrial hot dip plating conditions. Periodically remove samples for surface analysis and weight measurements.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and integrity via TEM/EDS
Microstructural analysis to check for interdiffusion
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-based RHEA rollers do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in weight loss and surface degradation (or fail to form a coherent and protective oxide layer) compared to the conventional steel rollers under identical test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

Abstract Although refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 . At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm 2 , which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date.
